analysis.one_liner: Funds nonprofit drug and device makers to sell essentials at cost-based prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral; it received no cosponsors and no committee or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would create a federal program to help nonprofit manufacturers make drugs and medical devices that are in short supply, made by only a few companies, or sold at high prices. Qualifying nonprofits would get federal grants and low-interest loans, have FDA fees waived, and get faster FDA review if they commit to selling at a price significantly below competing treatments. In exchange, they would have to sell at no more than 120% of their actual costs, publish their list prices, give the government first claim on part of their output during shortages, and cap executive pay at 40 times the lowest-paid worker's pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who rely on drugs with few manufacturers, drugs that have been in shortage, or drugs costing more than $50 a month; and nonprofit medicine makers (like hospital- and health-system-backed manufacturers) who would get capital, fee relief, and faster review to enter those markets.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients on scarce or costly drugs

how_it_helps.text: HHS would award cooperative agreements of up to $5 million and low-interest revolving loans of up to $5 million to nonprofit manufacturers of drugs and devices that have two or fewer active manufacturers, have appeared on the FDA shortage list, or cost more than $50 per month's supply [S3].

The bill writes tax-exempt nonprofit status into law for these manufacturers on the condition that they sell each product at a public list price no higher than 120% of production, research, regulatory, distribution, and financing costs [S3].
Qualifying nonprofits would be exempt from FDA prescription drug, generic drug, and medical device user fees, which are a real barrier to entry for small manufacturers [S3].
The FDA could grant priority review to a nonprofit's application if the sponsor commits to a specific price significantly lower than similar treatments on the market, shortening time to market [S3].

Recipients must cap top compensation at 40 times the lowest-paid employee's pay and give HHS priority purchase rights on at least 25% of production during shortages of the strategic national stockpile [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, who fund the grants and loans (the bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' for fiscal 2022 through 2031) and forgo the FDA user fees; and incumbent drug and device makers, who would face price-capped nonprofit competitors in their thinnest-competition markets.

drawbacks.text: The funding authorization is open-ended ('such sums as may be necessary' for ten years), so the total taxpayer cost was never fixed, and the bill directs CBO only to study later how savings could fund it [S3].

The program relies on HHS choosing which drugs and devices count as 'eligible' and which nonprofits get awards, which concentrates a great deal of judgment in one agency and invites lobbying over those choices [S3].

The cost-based price cap formula (120% of costs plus up to five years of research expenses) is complex and could be manipulated through how costs are allocated, and the projected savings to consumers and Medicare are speculative until products actually reach market [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacks a real problem — drug shortages and drugs with only one or two makers — by building a nonprofit, cost-plus competitor with government backing, rather than by capping prices directly. The main honest objections are that the taxpayer cost is open-ended, savings depend entirely on whether the supported products actually reach market and get prescribed, and the agency would have wide discretion over who wins the awards. It never got far enough for those tradeoffs to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in June 2021, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Jacky Rosen introduced the bill on June 24, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — is recorded before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent drug and device manufacturers, who faced no new taxpayer-backed nonprofit competitor, and no one else — patients saw no change.

for.name: Sen. Jacky Rosen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in June 2021 and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or committee vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senators besides the sponsor took a position, so the partisan shape of support or opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would create taxpayer-financed, price-capped nonprofit competitors specifically in markets with few manufacturers, shortages, or high prices — the markets where incumbent pricing power is strongest. It died before any such competition could form.
Nonprofit device makers would get the same grants, loans, fee waivers, and priority review to enter device markets with two or fewer manufacturers or persistent shortages.

industries.industry: Nonprofit medicine manufacturers (e.g., hospital-backed generic makers)
industries.note: These organizations would gain capital, waived FDA fees, and faster review to bring low-cost essentials to market; their gain is patients' gain by design, since their prices are capped near cost.
